lead.title: A family office with USD 1 billion or more now costs USD 6.6 million a year to run, and talent is the reason, J.P. Morgan finds
lead.standfirst: The bank's 2026 survey of 333 single-family offices shows costs climbing as families replace relatives with paid professionals.
lead.body:
The 2026 Global Family Office Report from J.P. Morgan Private Bank draws on 333 single-family offices in more than 30 countries, a sample 75 per cent larger than in 2024. Respondents have an average net worth of about USD 1.6 billion, and 59 per cent are based in the United States. It is one of the most detailed public pictures of what it costs to run the machinery that sits behind a great fortune.

For offices managing USD 1 billion or more, the average annual operating cost is USD 6.6 million, up from USD 6.1 million in the previous report. The scale is steep: about USD 0.9 million a year below USD 250 million, USD 1.7 million between USD 250 million and USD 500 million, and USD 3.3 million between USD 501 million and USD 999 million. The authors name talent as a major driver. Younger offices are often led by family members paid well below market rates, and costs rise as non-family professionals arrive. Investment teams are the most expensive, because they are paid at hedge fund and large asset manager levels.

Outsourcing is the other half of the picture. On average about 26 per cent of costs go to external providers, and more than four in ten offices spend at least 30 per cent externally. Legal work (about 52 per cent) and trading and execution (over 45 per cent) are the functions most often sent outside, along with cybersecurity. Compensation and staffing, financial administration and reporting tend to stay in house.

The pattern describes a profession in transition. As a family office moves from relatives to employees, it needs people who can run payroll, contracts, vendors and confidentiality as carefully as it runs a portfolio, and those functions are the ones families choose to keep close.
lead.why: Staffing and compensation are among the functions families keep in house, which is where a household or estate manager who understands contracts, vendors and discretion becomes part of the office rather than an adjunct to it.
lead.src: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report

articles.title: One in three family offices names over-reliance on a single person or provider as a continuity risk
articles.body:
Alongside its cost findings, the J.P. Morgan report asks family offices what could break their continuity. The external risks are familiar: financial market disruption (46 per cent) and regulatory and tax complexity (38 per cent). The internal list is more revealing. Family conflict or misaligned values, lack of succession planning, and over-reliance on one person or provider each draw 33 per cent.

The last of those is a staffing question as much as a governance one. An office that depends on a single trusted manager, a single assistant or a single outside firm is exposed the day that person leaves, falls ill or is simply approached by someone else. Families respond by documenting procedures, sharing knowledge across a small team and naming deputies.

Governance differs sharply among families that still own an operating company. About 6 in 10 respondents run a business alongside the office. Among them, 41 per cent rank internal conflict among their top three risks, and 20 per cent rank it first, about twice the rate of other families. Sixty-six per cent of business-owning families have a formal constitution or written bylaws, against about 50 per cent of the rest. The report recommends investment committees with outside advisers and fiduciary boards that may include non-family members.
articles.why: A house or estate manager who documents routines, trains a deputy and keeps clear records reduces exactly the single-person dependency that families now list as a risk.
articles.src: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, 2026 Global Family Office Report

articles.title: United States charter demand has risen 27 per cent in a year, Avinode reports, while departures stay stable
articles.body:
Avinode, the marketplace through which operators and brokers trade charter flights, reports that United States charter demand climbed 27 per cent over the past year, according to Aviation International News on 15 October. The subheadline adds that departures have remained stable despite an influx of United States based brokers.

The gap between the two measures is worth reading carefully. Demand measured in requests can grow faster than flights actually flown, particularly when more intermediaries are sending enquiries to the same pool of aircraft. For a principal's team, that can mean more quotes for the same trip, and more need to judge which quote is real.

Technology is entering the same space. FlyJets has taken its JetGPT charter agent out of an eight-month beta, with booking, listing and route alerts, AIN reported on 12 October. The detail of the tool was not available at the time of writing, but the direction is plain: first contact with a charter market is becoming automated.
articles.why: Whoever arranges a family's flights will increasingly compare automated quotes from many brokers, so judgement about operator quality, safety and true availability matters more than speed of response.

articles.title: Art Basel Paris opens its fifth edition under a new director, with 206 galleries and a record 12 joint booths
articles.body:
Art Basel Paris returns to the Grand Palais with preview days on 21 and 22 October and public days from 23 to 25 October. It is the first edition under director Karim Crippa. More than 200 exhibitors from 41 countries and territories take part, with more than 180 in the main Galeries sector, up from 177 last year, and a record 12 joint booths.

Nearly 30 galleries are new to the fair, among them ChertLüdde and Kraupa-Tuskany Zeidler from Berlin, Empty Gallery from Hong Kong, Luxembourg + Co. from London and Pace Di Donna Schrader from New York. More than 60 exhibitors operate spaces in France. Returning names include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, White Cube, Thaddaeus Ropac, Perrotin and Pace. An invitation-only Avant-Première is scheduled for 20 October.

The backdrop is a French market that the Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026 puts at USD 4.5 billion of sales in 2025, up 9 per cent on the year.
articles.why: Fair week means collectors, advisers and their staff converge on one city, and the person arranging the family's access, transport, security and shipping needs to know the calendar, and which days are invitation-only.
articles.src: USA Art News, citing Art Basel

briefs.t: Two thirds of family offices now plan for AI
briefs.b: J.P. Morgan finds that 65 per cent of surveyed single-family offices plan to prioritise AI investments, now or later. Some 43 per cent hold venture or growth equity, averaging 3.3 per cent of their portfolios.

briefs.t: Geopolitics tops the family office risk list
briefs.b: Geopolitics is the leading macro concern for 64 per cent of surveyed offices, ahead of interest rates (61 per cent) and growth (59 per cent). Only 28 per cent hold gold, at an average 0.9 per cent of assets.

briefs.t: Ocorian's family office report covers 25 jurisdictions
briefs.b: Published on 10 April 2026 in six parts, it examines governance, risk, data and AI, and the role of specialist providers to families.
